title: What is a standard operating procedure (SOP)?
seoTitle: What is a standard operating procedure?
description: A standard operating procedure (SOP) sets out the approved way to carry out a process. How SOPs relate to ISO 9001 documented information and training.
shortAnswer: A standard operating procedure (SOP) is a controlled document that sets out the approved way to carry out a recurring process, including its purpose, scope, responsibilities, steps and records. ISO 9000 defines a procedure as a specified way to carry out an activity or a process. In a quality or compliance system, an SOP is documented information: it is approved, versioned and reviewed, and people using it are trained on the current version.
keyTakeaways: ISO 9000:2015 defines a procedure as a "specified way to carry out an activity or a process"; an SOP is a documented, controlled procedure.
SOPs describe a process across roles; work instructions describe how one task is performed.
Under ISO 9001, SOPs are documented information and must be controlled, including version control.
Training on an SOP is only valid for the version trained; a revision can make prior training out of date.
ISO 9001:2026, the sixth edition, was published in September 2026 and keeps the documented information requirements.

blocks.text: SOP stands for standard operating procedure: a written description of how a recurring process must be carried out so that it is done consistently, safely and in line with requirements. "Standard" signals that it is the approved method, not one option among several.

The quality vocabulary standard [ISO 9000:2015](https://www.iso.org/standard/45481.html) defines a procedure (clause 3.4.5) as a "specified way to carry out an activity or a process", a definition reused in ISO 37301. A procedure can be documented or not; an SOP is the documented form. [ISO 9001](https://www.iso.org/standard/62085.html) treats such documents as documented information, which must be controlled so the right version is available where needed and protected from unintended change.

ISO 9001:2015 has been replaced by a sixth edition, [ISO 9001:2026](https://www.iso.org/standard/88464.html), published in September 2026. Certification bodies such as [DQS](https://www.dqsglobal.com/en/explore/focus-area/iso-9001-revision-at-a-glance) describe the changes as targeted, and documented information remains a core support requirement. Certified organizations should confirm transition timing with their certification body.

sections.heading: What does a standard operating procedure contain?

blocks.text: Most SOPs share a common structure, whatever the industry. The list below reflects common practice rather than a mandated template.

items: **Header and control data:** title, document number, version, effective date, owner, approver.
**Purpose:** why the process exists and what it achieves.
**Scope:** where, when and to whom it applies, and any exclusions.
**Definitions and references:** terms, related SOPs, [work instructions](/glossary/work-instruction), forms and the requirements the SOP satisfies.
**Procedure steps:** the sequence of activities, decision points and handovers.
**Records:** what evidence the process produces and where it is kept.
**Revision history:** what changed in each version and why.

sections.heading: How is an SOP different from a policy or a work instruction?

blocks.text: A policy states what the organization commits to and why. An SOP states how a process is carried out and by whom. A work instruction states exactly how one person performs one task within that process.

blocks.text: The boundary between an SOP and a work instruction varies between organizations. What matters is that each document has a clear owner and that the hierarchy is consistent.

sections.heading: How do SOPs connect to training?

blocks.text: Staff who follow an SOP need training on the current version, and that training needs to change when the SOP changes. Many regulated sectors, such as pharmaceutical manufacturing, expect a documented link between each SOP version and the people trained on it.

blocks.title: Illustrative example
blocks.text: A pathology laboratory revises its specimen labeling SOP from version 6 to version 7 to add a second identifier check. The training record shows 40 staff trained on version 6. Because the change affects a critical step, the laboratory reassigns a short practical check on the new step to those staff, rather than the full course. The numbers are illustrative.

Converting SOPs into learning is covered in [how to turn SOPs into training](/guides/how-to-convert-sops-into-training). Keeping the link between versions and training records is covered in [version control for training content](/guides/how-to-maintain-version-control-for-training-content).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry breaks an SOP into the concepts, decisions and steps a person must know and links each to assessment points. When an SOP version changes, only the affected steps and their assessments need review, and training records show which version each person was assessed against.

faqs.a: ISO 9001:2015 (clause 4.4.2) requires organizations, to the extent necessary, to maintain documented information to support the operation of processes and retain documented information to have confidence they are carried out as planned. It does not require a document called an SOP for every process. Organizations decide which processes need documented procedures.

faqs.q: How often should an SOP be reviewed?
faqs.a: At a set interval defined by the organization and whenever the process, equipment, risk or an external requirement changes. Many regulated organizations use a fixed cycle as a backstop, but a change driven review is what keeps SOPs accurate between cycles.

faqs.q: What is the difference between an SOP and a process map?
faqs.a: A process map shows the flow of a process visually, usually across roles. An SOP describes the steps, responsibilities, controls and records in text. Many SOPs include a process map as an attachment.

The people who perform the process, working with the process owner, usually draft it. A quality or compliance reviewer checks it against requirements, and an authorized approver releases it. Subject matter experts should also check the training derived from it.
